12519: Galatians: Who Belongs to Abraham's Family?
12520:
Galatians is Paul's most heated letter. There is no thanksgiving after the greeting, only a shocked 'I am astonished' (Gal 1:6). Young churches of non-Jews in central Asia Minor (modern Turkey) had been told by visiting teachers that trusting the Messiah Jesus was a good start, but that to belong fully to Abraham's family they must also be circumcised and take on the Jewish law: its food rules, its calendar, its way of life. Paul answers that this would turn the good news upside down.

For centuries Western Christians have read Galatians mainly as an answer to the question 'How can a guilty person be accepted by God?' That question is really in the letter (Gal 2:16, Gal 2:20). But the argument Paul actually fights in front of the Galatians is a related, more concrete one: who counts as God's people, and on what basis do Jews and non-Jews eat at one table (Gal 2:11-14, Gal 3:28-29)? Paul's answer is that God has acted in the cross of the Messiah to rescue the world from 'the present evil age' (Gal 1:4), to make one family out of Jews and Gentiles by trust in Jesus, and to give that family the Spirit, who produces the life the law pointed to (Gal 5:22-23).

This study reads the letter with its first hearers: former worshippers of Greek, Galatian and Roman gods who had stopped sacrificing to them, who were under pressure from their neighbours, and who were being offered what looked like a safer and more complete identity. It also lays out, side by side, the main ways modern scholars read the letter (traditional Protestant, the New Perspective, Paul within Judaism, apocalyptic and 'gift' readings), so you can weigh them yourself.
12521: Read Galatians as a family argument inside Israel's story. The question on the table is not whether Judaism was a religion of earning (Jews of Paul's day did not, in general, think so) but whether non-Jews who trust Israel's Messiah must become Jews to share Abraham's blessing. Paul answers from Israel's own scriptures: God promised Abraham that all nations would be blessed in him (Gen 12:3), God has now kept that promise through the Messiah's faithful death, and the Spirit poured out on uncircumcised Gentiles is God's own proof that they are already family. Grace (charis) is God's unearned gift that creates a relationship and calls for loyal response; faith (pistis) is trust and allegiance; the law is God's good gift with a specific, temporary role in the story until the Messiah came.
12523: The agitators asked, in effect, 'Are you really children of Abraham yet?' Paul answers that those who share Abraham's trust are his children, because God told Abraham the nations would be blessed in him. Membership, not merely private guilt, is the live issue.
12525: In Jewish thought the law was given to a people God had already rescued from Egypt; it was a way of living inside the relationship, not a ladder to climb into it. Paul does not deny that. He argues the law came 430 years after the promise and cannot add conditions to it, and that its role was to guard Israel until the Messiah came.
12526: The table is a test of the gospel
12527: In the ancient world, who you ate with showed who your people were. When Peter withdrew from eating with Gentile believers at Antioch, Paul said he was 'not walking straight toward the truth of the gospel'. The gospel creates a shared table.
12529: Greek pistis covers belief, trust, faithfulness and loyalty. In Galatians it marks those who rely on the Messiah and stay loyal to him, and possibly also the Messiah's own faithfulness to God. Faith that matters is 'faith working through love'.
12530: Grace as gift that creates a bond
12531: In Greco-Roman and Jewish settings a gift (charis) created a relationship and invited a grateful, loyal response. John Barclay shows that Paul's stress is that God's gift in Christ was given without regard to prior worth: to Gentiles, to a former persecutor, to people with no ethnic or moral 'qualification'. It is free but not cheap: it creates a new way of life.
12532: A new age has broken in
12533: Paul frames everything by the arrival of a new age: Jesus 'gave himself to rescue us from the present evil age' and what counts now is 'new creation'. Jewish hope for the age to come, with the Spirit poured out, has begun.
12535: Children, heirs, slaves, guardians, adoption, brothers and sisters: Paul thinks with the ancient household. The Spirit who cries 'Abba, Father' makes former outsiders into sons and heirs, as Israel was called God's son.
12537: Crucifixion was the most shameful death in the Roman world and, by Deuteronomy, a sign of curse. Paul makes the crucified Messiah his only boast, and refuses to boast in circumcision as a mark of status.
12538: Gentile believers (former worshippers of the gods)
12539: Whether they truly belong to God's people without circumcision; social and legal pressure after abandoning their city's gods and the emperor's honours; how to live a holy life without the law's clear rules.
12541: Faithfulness to the covenant of circumcision given to Abraham (Gen 17); the good order and reputation of the community; perhaps avoiding persecution for welcoming uncircumcised Gentiles (Gal 6:12).
12543: How to keep faith with their own heritage while eating with Gentile brothers and sisters; whether Paul despises the law (he insists he does not, Gal 3:21, Gal 5:14).
12544: Wider audience: Jerusalem and Antioch circles who would hear of the letter
12545: Paul's standing as an apostle, his relationship to Peter and James, and whether his mission undermined Jewish identity.
12547: Paul opens by declaring that Jesus gave himself for our sins to rescue us from the present evil age. The whole letter flows from this: something decisive has already happened.
12549: Turning to a 'gospel' that requires circumcision is not an upgrade but a desertion of the God who called them.
12551: Paul tells his story: zealous persecutor, then called like a prophet to announce the Son among the nations. His message did not come from Jerusalem.
12553: The pillars accepted Titus uncircumcised and shook hands on Paul's mission. But at Antioch Peter withdrew from table fellowship, and Paul confronted him publicly.
12555: Even Jews by birth are put right with God not by works of the law but through the faith/faithfulness of Jesus Christ. Paul has died to the law and now lives by the Son who loved him.
12556: You received the Spirit by hearing
12557: The Galatians' own experience proves the point: God gave them the Spirit and worked miracles when they heard and trusted, not when they kept the law.
12559: Abraham trusted God; Scripture foresaw the nations blessed in him. The Messiah absorbed the curse so that Abraham's blessing and the Spirit reach the Gentiles. The promise to the one 'seed' is fulfilled in Christ.
12560: Why the law? A guardian until Messiah
12561: The law came later, could not cancel the promise, and served as a paidagogos, a household guardian, until the Messiah. Now all, Jew and Greek, slave and free, male and female, are one in him, adopted heirs with the Spirit.
12562: Do not go back; two mothers
12563: Paul pleads as a mother in labour pains. Then he reads the Hagar and Sarah story as a picture of two covenants and two ways of being family: slavery and freedom.
12565: Christ set us free; do not take on slavery again. But freedom is not licence: it is freedom to be slaves of one another in love, which fulfils the whole law. Walk by the Spirit.
12567: The Spirit's community restores the fallen gently, shares goods with teachers, and keeps sowing good, especially within the household of faith.
12568: New creation and the Israel of God
12569: In his own large handwriting Paul sums up: neither circumcision nor uncircumcision counts, but new creation. Peace and mercy on those who walk by this rule, and on the Israel of God.
12570: No other gospel: Paul's call came from God
12571: Paul greets the churches as an apostle sent 'not from men' but by Jesus Christ and God the Father, and announces that Jesus gave himself to rescue us from the present evil age. Instead of the usual thanksgiving he expresses astonishment that the Galatians are deserting the one who called them for a different 'gospel', and pronounces a curse on anyone, even an angel, who preaches otherwise. He then tells his own story: a zealous persecutor of the church, he was set apart by God before birth and called to proclaim the Son among the nations. He did not consult anyone, went to Arabia, returned to Damascus, and only after three years visited Peter in Jerusalem for fifteen days.
12572: Where were the Galatian churches? 'Galatia' could mean the ethnic region in the north around Ancyra (modern Ankara), settled by Celtic Gauls in the 200s BC, or the larger Roman province, which in Paul's day stretched south to include Pisidian Antioch, Iconium, Lystra and Derbe. The North Galatian view (J. B. Lightfoot, Hans Dieter Betz, J. Louis Martyn, Martinus de Boer) holds that Paul wrote to ethnic Galatians he evangelised on his second or third journey (Acts 16:6, Acts 18:23), probably in the mid-50s. The South Galatian view (William Ramsay, F. F. Bruce, Richard Longenecker, Ben Witherington) holds he wrote to the cities he founded on his first journey with Barnabas (Acts 13-14), which would allow an early date, perhaps around AD 48, before the Jerusalem council of Acts 15. Acts records no visit by Paul to cities in the north. The question matters for how Galatians relates to Acts and to Romans, but not for the letter's main message.
12573: Ancient letters normally opened with a thanksgiving to the gods or for the recipients. Leaving it out was a deliberate social snub: hearers would feel the chill. The curse formula ('let him be anathema') draws on the Old Testament idea of something devoted to God for destruction. Paul's appeal to his own story fits ancient rhetoric: a speaker established his character (ēthos) before making his case. His language of 'pleasing men' versus being a 'slave of Christ' (Gal 1:10) touches the patronage world, where clients flattered patrons for favour.
12574: Paul describes his past 'in Judaism' with pride and pain: he advanced beyond his peers and was extremely zealous for the ancestral traditions (Gal 1:14). 'Zeal' recalls Phinehas and the Maccabees, who used force to defend Israel's covenant boundaries (Num 25:11-13). His call is told in the language of Israel's prophets: set apart 'from my mother's womb' like the servant of Isaiah 49 and Jeremiah. He did not abandon Israel's God; he was sent by Israel's God to be the servant who brings light to the nations. 'Rescue from the present evil age' uses Jewish apocalyptic language of two ages: this age under evil powers and the age to come.
12575: Gentile hearers, many of whom had recently been told by impressive visitors that Paul's message was incomplete or second-hand, would hear Paul insisting that his gospel is not a diluted copy of Jerusalem's. They would also feel the shock of the curse: this is not a minor disagreement over practice but about the very identity of the good news. Some may have felt caught between loyalty to Paul, their founder, and respect for teachers with links to Jerusalem.
12576: The chapter asks what the core of the good news is and how it relates to the additions communities make to it. It also shows that a person can be zealous, sincere and well-educated in Scripture and still be opposing God's purposes; Paul's story is a call to humility. His independence is not individualism: he still went to Jerusalem and sought fellowship (Gal 2:2).
12577: The servant called 'from the womb' to bring God's salvation to the end of the earth; Paul sees his mission to the nations in this role.
12578: Jeremiah set apart before birth as a prophet to the nations.
12579: Phinehas's zeal for God's covenant, the model for Paul's former violent zeal.
12580: Warnings against prophets who lead the people away from God, background to Paul's curse on a false gospel.
12581: Paul converted from Judaism to Christianity on the Damascus road, leaving his old religion.
12582: Paul tells a prophetic call within Israel's story: the same God now revealed his Son to him and sent him to the nations. He changed his mind about Jesus and about the Gentiles, not his God.
12583: Jerusalem, Antioch and the truth of the gospel
12584: Fourteen years later Paul went to Jerusalem with Barnabas and Titus, an uncircumcised Greek, and privately set his gospel before the leaders. Titus was not compelled to be circumcised, despite 'false brothers'. James, Cephas (Peter) and John, the 'pillars', recognised Paul's mission to the uncircumcised and asked only that he remember the poor. But later at Antioch, Peter, who had been eating with Gentile believers, withdrew when 'certain people from James' arrived, and even Barnabas followed. Paul confronted Peter publicly. He then states the principle: even Jews by birth know that a person is justified not by works of the law but through faith in (or the faithfulness of) Jesus Christ. 'I have been crucified with Christ; I no longer live, but Christ lives in me.'
12585: Is the Jerusalem visit of Gal 2:1-10 the council of Acts 15? Many scholars think so: both involve Paul, Barnabas, circumcision and the Jerusalem leaders. Others, especially South Galatian advocates, identify it with the famine-relief visit of Acts 11:27-30, which would date Galatians before the council and explain why Paul never mentions the council's decision (Acts 15:23-29), which would have been his strongest argument. The Antioch incident probably happened in the late 40s. Antioch in Syria was a large mixed city where Jews and Gentiles in the Jesus movement had been eating together (Acts 11:19-26). Pressure from Judea, where Jewish nationalism was rising under Roman rule in the 40s, may explain why the visitors from James wanted Jewish believers to keep clearer separation.
12586: In Mediterranean society, meals expressed belonging and rank. To share a table was to accept someone as family or friend; to withdraw was a public statement. Paul's public rebuke of Peter 'before them all' was an honour challenge between two leading men. Paul's handshake with the pillars (the 'right hand of fellowship') was a formal sign of agreement and partnership in the ancient world.
12587: Jews in the diaspora regularly mixed with Gentiles, but table fellowship raised questions: was the food kosher, had it been offered to idols, was the wine poured as a libation? Jews held a range of views. The issue at Antioch was probably not that Peter ate pork but the degree of intimacy and the status of Gentile believers: were they full members or guests? Paul's phrase 'Jews by birth and not Gentile sinners' (Gal 2:15) uses a common Jewish way of speaking, where 'sinners' meant those outside the covenant law. Paul then says that even Jews rely on the Messiah for righteousness, so the table cannot be divided along that line. 'Crucified with Christ' is covenant participation: what happened to the Messiah is counted as happening to his people.
12588: The Galatians would recognise their own situation: Gentiles being told they were second-class unless they adopted Jewish practice. They would hear that even Peter had wobbled under social pressure, and that Paul had stood for their equal place at the table. The words 'the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me' would land with warmth for people who were feeling unwanted.
12589: Who eats with whom is still a gospel issue: churches can be divided by race, class, politics or culture while believing the same creed. Paul calls a withdrawal from shared fellowship 'not walking straight toward the truth of the gospel'. The chapter also holds together social and personal faith: 'he loved me and gave himself for me' is one of the most personal lines in the New Testament.
12590: 'No one living is righteous before you': Paul's 'by works of the law no flesh will be justified' echoes this psalm.
12591: Daniel refusing the king's food: an example of food laws as faithful Jewish identity in a foreign setting.
12592: The covenant of circumcision with Abraham, the strongest scriptural argument the agitators could make for circumcising Gentiles.
12593: Peter fell into legalism, trying to earn salvation by keeping rules, and Paul corrected his theology.
12594: Peter did not change his doctrine; he changed his table under social pressure. Paul says this 'hypocrisy' denied in practice what both of them believed: that Jews and Gentiles are equally put right with God through the Messiah, and so belong at one table.
12595: Abraham's family, the curse and the promise
12596: 'You foolish Galatians!' Paul asks whether they received the Spirit by works of the law or by hearing with faith. Then he turns to Abraham, who 'believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness'. Scripture foresaw that God would justify the nations by faith and announced the gospel beforehand: 'In you shall all the nations be blessed.' Those who rely on works of the law are under a curse, but the Messiah redeemed us from the curse by becoming a curse, so that Abraham's blessing might come to the Gentiles and we might receive the promised Spirit. The law, coming 430 years later, cannot annul the promise. It was added because of transgressions and served as a guardian until Christ. Now all are children of God through faith; in Christ there is neither Jew nor Greek, slave nor free, male and female, and all are Abraham's seed and heirs.
12597: The agitators likely had a strong scriptural case: God's covenant with Abraham required circumcision for all males in his household, including foreigners (Gen 17:9-14), and Abraham was a model of obedience. Jewish writers such as the author of *Jubilees* and Philo honoured Abraham as the first to turn from idols. Paul answers on their ground, reading the Abraham story in order: trust and blessing for the nations (Gen 12, Gen 15) before circumcision (Gen 17) and long before Sinai.
12598: 'Who has bewitched you?' (Gal 3:1) uses the language of the evil eye, a widely feared form of envious magic in the ancient world; Paul hints the visitors have cast a spell on them. 'Publicly portrayed as crucified' uses the word for a public poster or notice. A will or covenant (diathēkē) once ratified could not be altered by a later party (Gal 3:15). The paidagōgos was a household slave who escorted a boy to school and supervised him until adulthood; he was protective but often remembered as strict. When the son came of age, the guardian's job was over.
12599: Paul's argument is a chain of scriptural texts read the way Jewish teachers read them, linking passages by shared words: Gen 15:6 and Hab 2:4 (both 'faith' and 'righteous'), Deut 27:26 and Deut 21:23 (both 'cursed'). Deuteronomy's curse was not only individual: Israel as a nation had experienced the covenant curses of exile (Deut 28-30). N. T. Wright argues Paul sees the Messiah taking Israel's curse on himself so that the blessing of Abraham can finally flow to the nations; others read the curse as the universal plight of all who break God's law. The 'seed' (Gal 3:16) is singular because the promise culminates in one representative, the Messiah, in whom many are one.
12600: The Galatians had seen miracles and received the Spirit (Gal 3:5); Paul reminds them that God had already accepted them as they were. To people being told they were not yet Abraham's children, the closing line would be a lifeline: 'If you are Christ's, then you are Abraham's offspring, heirs according to promise.' Slaves and women in the house church would hear the baptismal formula of 3:28 as an astonishing statement of belonging.
12601: The chapter grounds identity not in ethnicity, achievement or social rank but in belonging to the Messiah. It challenges churches that quietly rank members, and individuals who feel they have to earn a place. It also models reading the Old Testament as one story leading to Christ, not as an obsolete book.
12602: Abraham believed the Lord, who counted it to him as righteousness: Paul's anchor text.
12603: All the families of the earth blessed in Abraham: Paul calls this 'the gospel preached beforehand'.
12604: The righteous shall live by faith(fulness): read by Paul of life given through trust.
12605: Cursed is everyone who does not keep all the law; part of the covenant blessings and curses.
12606: A hanged man is cursed by God; Paul applies it to the crucified Messiah.
12607: The law was a schoolmaster that teaches us we are sinners so that we run to Christ for salvation.
12608: The paidagōgos was a babysitter-guardian, not a teacher. Paul's main point is historical: the law had a temporary guardianship over Israel 'until faith came', that is, until the Messiah arrived. Now that he has come, Jews and Gentiles alike are heirs without that guardian. (The law's role in revealing sin is real but secondary here.)
12609: From slaves to heirs; Hagar and Sarah
12610: An heir who is a child is no better than a slave, under guardians until the date set by his father. So we too were enslaved under the 'elements of the world'. But when the fullness of time came, God sent his Son, born of a woman, born under the law, to redeem those under the law so that we might receive adoption. Because you are sons, God sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts crying 'Abba, Father'. Paul asks how they can turn back to weak elements, observing days, months, seasons and years. He recalls their warm welcome when he first came to them ill, and pleads as a mother in labour until Christ is formed in them. He closes with an allegory: Abraham had two sons, one by the slave Hagar and one by the free woman Sarah; these represent two covenants, and believers are children of the free woman.
12611: Gal 4:10 ('days, months, seasons, years') is usually read as the Jewish sabbath, new moons and festivals the agitators were urging. Bruce Winter and Justin Hardin argue that the imperial cult is also in view: cities across the province of Galatia held festivals honouring Augustus and his successors, and Gentiles who had stopped joining them but were not recognised Jews were socially and perhaps legally exposed. Becoming Jewish proselytes through circumcision would give them a recognised status, since Jews were traditionally exempted from civic worship. This reading is debated, but it explains why Paul says the agitators want to avoid persecution (Gal 6:12). Paul's illness on his first visit (Gal 4:13-15) is unknown; suggestions include an eye problem or malaria.
12612: Roman law placed a fatherless heir under a tutor and a curator until a set age; Paul adapts this. Roman adoption (adoptio) transferred a person fully into a new family, cancelling old debts and giving full rights of inheritance; adoptions of adult heirs were common among the elite, including emperors. 'Abba' is Aramaic for 'father', the word of a family member, preserved in Greek-speaking churches (Mark 14:36). Welcoming a messenger 'as an angel of God' reflects ancient hospitality codes. Ancient writers, Jewish (Philo) and Greek, used allegory to draw spiritual meaning from stories; Paul explicitly says he is doing this (Gal 4:24).
12613: Israel was God's 'firstborn son' (Exod 4:22), redeemed from slavery in Egypt. Paul retells the exodus: God 'sent' his Son and 'sent' his Spirit to redeem slaves and make them heirs, as God once brought Israel out of slavery. His allegory reverses the usual association (Isaac and Sarah were Israel's ancestors) to make the point that what counts is promise and Spirit, not natural descent. He quotes Isa 54:1, where barren Zion rejoices after exile because her children will be many: the restoration promised to Israel is happening as the nations come in. 'The present Jerusalem' probably refers to the Jerusalem-based mission that insisted on circumcising Gentiles, not to the Jewish people as such; Martyn reads the two mothers as two Gentile missions.
